prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "ROYAL BANK OF CANADA" (ticker RY). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?

   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?

   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?

   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?

   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: RBC is a top-dog bank in Canada's five-bank oligopoly, with strong momentum (+35.5% over 52 weeks) and a respected CEO, but it is not a leader in an emerging industry and has no single Rule Breaker innovation, so it fits Gardner's Rule Breaker approach poorly and his Rule Maker idea better.
summaries.buffett: RBC has the kind of durable, understandable franchise Buffett likes in banks: low-cost sticky deposits, a dominant position, a 16.3% ROE in FY2025 and dividends paid since 1870. The trade-offs are high leverage typical of banks and a price near 2.6x book and 17x trailing earnings, which leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value RBC's oligopoly position, conservative culture and steady compounding, but would invert and worry about leverage, Canadian housing exposure and a full price; it is a quality franchise rather than an obvious bargain.
summaries.lynch: RBC is a classic stalwart: a big, steady grower whose diluted EPS rose from C$7.82 in FY2020 to C$14.07 in FY2025. At about 16x forward earnings against roughly 13-14% expected EPS growth plus a 2.6% dividend yield, it is fairly priced rather than a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: RBC scores well on Fisher's points for management depth, sales strength and long-term outlook, and it has invested in digital and AI ahead of peers, but as a bank it has limited room for new products to drive growth well above the economy.
summaries.graham: RBC passes Graham's tests for size, a long profit record and an unbroken dividend going back over 150 years, but fails on price: a trailing P/E of about 17 and price-to-book of about 2.6 give P/E x P/B near 45, double Graham's 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: RBC does not fit Thiel's Zero to One model: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and operates in a mature, regulated oligopoly rather than a new market it created, even if that oligopoly is durable.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on growth, efficiency and big platform shifts; RBC shows good operating leverage (FY2025 revenue +16.2% vs expenses +6.8%) and an AI push, but it is a mature bank, not a prime beneficiary of a major technology shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: RBC's earnings momentum (record results, adjusted EPS up 11% in Q3 2026) and a recovering capital markets cycle fit Druckenmiller's focus on improving earnings, but bank stocks are highly sensitive to rates, credit and the Canadian economy amid US tariff risk.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith generally avoids banks because of leverage and dependence on outside factors, so RBC, despite its quality and 16-18% ROE, falls outside his good-company criteria of high returns on unleveraged capital and low capital needs.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula excludes financial firms like banks, and RBC's 'return on capital' and earnings yield (about 5.9%) cannot be measured on Greenblatt's terms, so it is not a fit.
summaries.akre: RBC has a good business and an able, long-serving CEO, two of Akre's three legs, but its ability to reinvest capital at high rates is limited by bank capital rules and Canada's mature market.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses at deep discounts during temporary trouble; RBC is simple and durable but trades near record highs at about 2.6x book, with no fixable setback creating a bargain.
summaries.wood: RBC is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense; it is an incumbent that disruptors in fintech and digital banking target, so it does not fit Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: RBC matches Ackman's taste for simple, predictable, dominant businesses with high barriers to entry, but its leverage, exposure to interest rates and credit cycles, and full valuation weaken the fit.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model is only partly visible at RBC: scale lowers its costs, but it keeps the savings as high margins rather than passing them back to customers in the way Costco or Amazon do.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed new companies in huge emerging markets; a 160-year-old bank in a mature market is far from Sequoia's style.
summaries.nash: RBC passes Nash's quality and safety screens on scale, profitability and a 0.18% short interest, but fails several hard ones: revenue growth is about 9% (under 10%), bank leverage means it would fail the banker's-lending test, and its free cash flow is not meaningful, scoring about 70 of 130 on his 13 categories.

momentum.evidence: RBC's NYSE shares rose 35.5% over the 52 weeks to mid-October 2026, to about US$192 from a 52-week low of US$143.13, well ahead of most broad indexes.

g4.evidence: CEO Dave McKay has led RBC since 2014 with record results, but RBC is a widely held bank (about 47% institutional ownership) without a famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate RBC a Buy with a US$207.86 average target, and it is seen as a premium-priced but fairly valued bank rather than commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: RBC is a long-established bank whose five segments (personal, commercial, wealth, insurance, capital markets) a careful generalist can understand, though trading and credit risks need care.

b2.evidence: RBC has been profitable every year in modern history, earning C$11,437M even in pandemic-hit FY2020 and C$20,369M in FY2025.

integrity.evidence: RBC is well governed and returns capital rationally (C$1.6B of buybacks and C$2.4B of dividends in Q3 2026), but in 2024 it fired its CFO over an undisclosed personal relationship and preferential treatment.

b6.evidence: RBC avoids frenzied deals, but its C$13.5B HSBC Canada purchase (2024) and US City National expansion show it does grow by acquisition.

roic.evidence: ROE is high for a bank at 16.3% in FY2025 and 17.5% in the first nine months of FY2026, but it depends on bank leverage of about 16x liabilities to equity.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank (reported operating cash flow swings with deposits and trading); RBC's capacity is better shown by the C$4.0B it returned to shareholders in Q3 2026.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings helped lift diluted EPS from C$7.82 in FY2020 to C$14.07 in FY2025, and ROE rose from 14.2% to 16.3% over the same period.

safety.evidence: At about 17x trailing earnings and 2.6x book value, the shares trade near analysts' average target of US$207.86, leaving no meaningful margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 15.9 against consensus FY2026 EPS growth of 13.6% and a 2.6% dividend yield is reasonable for RBC's quality but not cheap versus Canadian peers.

mu5.evidence: RBC's diversification and 13.5% CET1 ratio make failure unlikely, but leverage, a severe Canadian housing or credit crisis, or a trading loss are real ways a bank can be badly hurt.

reinvest.evidence: RBC can reinvest at mid-teens ROE in US wealth, commercial banking and capital markets, but capital rules and a mature home market cap how much it can deploy.

ly2.evidence: RBC is a clear stalwart: a large, steadily growing bank with a simple story of compounding earnings and dividends.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 17 is above the expected EPS growth rate of about 13.6% for FY2026, even before adding the 2.6% yield.

runway.evidence: Revenue grew 16.2% in FY2025 helped by HSBC Canada and 9.2% in the first nine months of FY2026, but long-term growth is tied to the Canadian economy plus US wealth expansion.

ly7.evidence: RBC is shrinking its share count (diluted shares 1,391.1M in Q3 2026 vs 1,409.7M a year earlier, after C$1.6B of Q3 buybacks), but there is no notable insider open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: RBC is Canada's largest company by market value and is heavily covered by Wall Street and Bay Street analysts.

fi2.evidence: RBC keeps launching digital and AI tools (NOMI, Avion, Borealis AI research), but banking products change slowly.

fi3.evidence: RBC's technology and AI spending has helped it rank near the top of the Evident AI Index of global banks, but the earnings payoff is hard to isolate.

fi4.evidence: RBC is Canada's leader in wealth management and investment banking and cross-sells across 19+ million clients, showing strong sales capability.

longterm.evidence: RBC invested in AI and digital years before peers and took a long-term view buying HSBC Canada, while still managing closely to quarterly ROE targets.

gr1.evidence: RBC has C$2,498,817M of assets and a market value of about US$267B, making it Canada's largest company.

ni10.evidence: RBC has reported a profit in every one of the last ten fiscal years, including C$11,437M in pandemic-hit FY2020.

gr4.evidence: RBC has paid dividends every year since 1870 and declared C$6.04 per share in FY2025.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from C$7.82 in FY2020 to C$14.07 in FY2025 alone, an 80% rise, well beyond one third over ten years.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 17.2 is above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 17.2 times P/B of about 2.6 gives about 45, double Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: RBC's products are similar to those of TD and the other big banks, with no technology ten times better.

timing.evidence: A recovering capital markets cycle and steadier credit help now, with record Q3 2026 net income of C$6,024M, but rate cuts and US tariffs on Canada are headwinds.

th3.evidence: RBC grew over 160 years in a large national banking market rather than by dominating a small niche first.

team.evidence: RBC's management, led by CEO Dave McKay since 2014, is highly regarded among banks but is not a founder-led, world-class innovation team.

th5.evidence: RBC has Canada's largest branch, adviser and digital distribution network, reaching more than 19 million clients.

durable.evidence: Canada's tightly regulated five-bank structure and RBC's scale make its position very likely to hold for 10-20 years, despite fintech challengers.

th7.evidence: RBC competes in well-understood markets and has no secret opportunity others fail to see.

trend.evidence: RBC is an early AI adopter among banks, but it is a user rather than a leading beneficiary of a platform shift.

dr1.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 diluted EPS rose to C$12.10 from C$10.31, and consensus FY2026 adjusted EPS of C$16.39 implies 13.6% growth.

dr2.evidence: Further HSBC Canada synergies, buybacks and US wealth growth could lift results, but much of this is already expected by analysts.

dr4.evidence: A steeper yield curve and stabilising credit help, but Bank of Canada rate cuts and tariff pressure on the Canadian economy work against it.

dr6.evidence: Q4 FY2026 results due in early December 2026, a likely dividend increase and continued buybacks are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: As a leveraged, rate-sensitive bank with valuation near analysts' targets, RBC is better suited to a core holding than a large concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is not meaningful for a bank; its 30.6% FY2025 net margin is high and points to moderate pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Bank free cash flow is not meaningful (reported FCF is negative from balance-sheet growth); the earnings yield of about 5.9% is a better gauge.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not a meaningful measure for a bank whose deposits and debt are operating items.

pa2.evidence: RBC is posting record results (Q3 2026 net income C$6,024M, ROE 17.9%) and is not in a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: With a 13.5% CET1 ratio, diversified earnings and its systemic importance in Canada, the chance of permanent loss on RBC is low.

wo1.evidence: RBC is a bank, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing, though it uses AI internally.

wo2.evidence: Banking costs do not fall quickly with volume; RBC's non-interest expense rose 6.8% to C$36,592M in FY2025.

wo3.evidence: RBC does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: RBC's addressable market grows with the economy and wealth, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: RBC's earnings depend heavily on interest rates, credit conditions and capital markets activity.

ns1.evidence: RBC keeps its scale savings as a 30.6% net margin rather than passing them to customers through lower fees or better rates.

ns4.evidence: RBC's position should strengthen modestly with HSBC Canada and US wealth growth, but not clearly beyond today's already strong standing.

va2.evidence: Safe savings, mortgages and business credit solve real, large needs, but many banks solve them equally well.

tn1.evidence: RBC is a traditional bank adopting AI, not a company built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees RBC as a high-quality Canadian bank, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation story.

tn3.evidence: RBC is a US$267B large-cap Canadian bank, outside small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in four of the last five years (to C$66,605M in FY2025) and it is highly profitable, but as a bank it carries far more liabilities than cash, a valid structural reason for the miss.

tn5.evidence: Quarterly free cash flow and cash-versus-debt are not meaningful for a bank whose cash flows swing with deposits and trading.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 9.2% in the first nine months of FY2026 (C$53,951M vs C$49,396M), just under 10%, after 16.2% in FY2025 with HSBC Canada.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 9% plus a non-meaningful (negative reported) free-cash-flow margin falls well short of 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue rose 16.2% to C$66,605M while non-interest expense rose 6.8% to C$36,592M.

tn9.evidence: RBC trips the revenue-growth kill (9.2% in nine-month FY2026, down from 16.2% in FY2025) and, as a bank, liabilities far exceed cash.

tn10.evidence: RBC faces ongoing OSFI capital rules, scrutiny of bank fees and US regulatory oversight of its wealth and City National units, though nothing currently threatens the business.

tn11.evidence: RBC provides banking, wealth and capital markets services that help households and businesses save, borrow and invest, and charges interest spreads and fees; clients choose it for safety, scale and breadth.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 5, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in FY2022 (C$48,985M vs C$49,693M), margins swung, and bank free cash flow is not consistently positive.

tn15.evidence: As a bank, RBC's total liabilities of C$2,353,723M are about 16x its C$145,094M of equity (July 31, 2026), far above the 4x test.

tn18.evidence: McKay has 12 years as CEO and a strong record of growth (net income up from C$11,437M in FY2020 to C$20,369M in FY2025), but he is not a founder and has made no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: RBC beat consensus in Q4 FY2025 and has posted a run of record quarters, though it has not beaten in every quarter.

tn21.evidence: No accounting or auditor issues and margins are rising, but the 2024 firing of CFO Nadine Ahn over an undisclosed relationship is a governance blemish.

tn22.evidence: RBC has large real revenue (C$66,605M in FY2025), strong profits and is buying back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: At about 17x earnings with a 2.6% yield the price implies mid-to-high single-digit earnings growth, below recent EPS growth of about 17% in nine-month FY2026, but that pace is unlikely to last.

tn25.evidence: Nash's free-cash-flow DCF cannot be applied meaningfully to a bank, whose reported free cash flow is driven by balance-sheet flows.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 15.9 against 13.6% expected EPS growth gives a PEG of about 1.2, slightly above 1 and at a premium to Canadian bank peers.
